A complete workflow

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/workflow.Rmd
workflow.Rmd

A variable-order Markov chain describes a process in which the amount of history needed to predict the next state depends on the history itself. The model is stored as a prediction suffix tree: every node is a context, a run of recent states, with a distribution over the next state, and a context is kept only where the data support it (Ron, Singer, & Tishby, 1996; Bühlmann & Wyner, 1999). Fitting such a tree is one step of an analysis that also has to decide how deep the tree may grow, which of its contexts are reliable, how well it predicts data it has not seen, and whether two groups of sequences differ.

This guide takes one event log through the whole analysis: reading the data, fitting the tree, reading its pathways, smoothing and pruning, choosing the depth by cross-validation, assessing fit, checking the reliability of the pathways with the bootstrap, predicting next states, and comparing two groups. Each step is treated briefly; the specialized guides give the detail: data input, smoothing and pruning, model selection, pathway reliability, prediction and scoring, comparing groups and visualization.

library(transitiontrees)

Data

group_regulation_long is an event log of collaborative regulation of learning: each row is one regulation move made by a student working in a small group. The data are synthetic, generated for the tna package from its group_regulation data; they serve as a well-structured example and are not evidence about students.

  • Actor: Actor, the student; one sequence is built per student and session.
  • Time: Time, the time stamp of the move (POSIXct), used to order the moves and to split sessions.
  • State: Action, the regulation move, one of nine codes (adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis).
  • Group covariate: Achiever, whether the student is a high or a low achiever; used in the group comparison.
  • Other columns: Group (the collaboration group) and Course; not used here.
head(group_regulation_long)
#>   Actor Achiever Group Course                Time    Action
#> 1     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:27:07  cohesion
#> 2     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:35:20 consensus
#> 3     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:42:18   discuss
#> 4     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:50:00 synthesis
#> 5     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:52:25     adapt
#> 6     1     High     1      A 2025-01-01 08:57:31 consensus
with(group_regulation_long,
     c(events = length(Actor), students = length(unique(Actor)),
       groups = length(unique(Group)), courses = length(unique(Course))))
#>   events students   groups  courses 
#>    27533     2000      200        3

The log holds 27,533 moves by 2,000 students in 200 groups and three courses.

Fitting the tree

context_tree() reads the long log directly when the state column is named in action. The moves of each actor are ordered by time, and a gap of more than time_threshold seconds (default 900) starts a new session. The tree below allows histories of up to three moves and gives a context its own node when it occurs at least ten times.

tree <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                     actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                     max_depth = 3, min_count = 10)
tree
#> <transitiontrees>  377 nodes, depth <= 3, 9 states  [unpruned]
#>   alphabet : adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis
#>   fit on   : 2000 sequences, 27533 observations
#>   smoothing: floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate)   min_count = 10
#> (start)   n=27533  -> consensus (0.25)
#> |-- adapt     n=509    -> consensus (0.47)
#> |   |-- consensus  n=27     -> cohesion (0.48)
#> |   |-- coregulate  n=28     -> consensus (0.50)
#> |   |   `-- consensus  n=21     -> consensus (0.43)
#> |   |-- discuss   n=259    -> consensus (0.47)
#> |   |   |-- consensus  n=60     -> consensus (0.53)
#> |   |   |-- coregulate  n=37     -> consensus (0.43)
#> |   |   |-- discuss   n=48     -> consensus (0.52)
#> |   |   |-- emotion   n=14     -> consensus (0.50)
#> |   |   |-- monitor   n=25     -> consensus (0.40)
#> |   |   `-- plan      n=26     -> consensus (0.42)
#> |   |-- monitor   n=16     -> consensus (0.50)
#> |   `-- synthesis  n=140    -> consensus (0.48)
#> |       `-- discuss   n=107    -> consensus (0.45)
#> |-- cohesion  n=1695   -> consensus (0.50)
#> |   |-- adapt     n=130    -> consensus (0.54)
#> |   |   |-- consensus  n=13     -> consensus (0.61)
#> |   |   |-- discuss   n=65     -> consensus (0.55)
#> |   |   `-- synthesis  n=32     -> consensus (0.56)
#> |   |-- cohesion  n=45     -> consensus (0.42)
#> |   |   `-- emotion   n=24     -> consensus (0.46)
#> |   |-- consensus  n=84     -> consensus (0.51)
#> |   |   |-- cohesion  n=11     -> plan (0.45)
#> |   |   |-- discuss   n=13     -> consensus (0.61)
#> |   |   |-- emotion   n=11     -> consensus (0.45) 
#> ... 351 more nodes (use as.data.frame(x) or summary(x))

The banner reports 2,000 sequences, one per student, and 27,533 observed moves. The unpruned tree has 377 contexts. The first line of the tree is the root, (start): the next-move distribution with no history, in which consensus is the most likely move with probability 0.25. Every deeper context is judged against the prediction of its parent.

The root distribution is the marginal frequency of each move.

state_frequencies(tree)
#>        state count proportion
#> 1  consensus  6797     0.2469
#> 2       plan  6623     0.2405
#> 3    discuss  4267     0.1550
#> 4    emotion  3075     0.1117
#> 5 coregulate  2133     0.0775
#> 6   cohesion  1839     0.0668
#> 7    monitor  1516     0.0551
#> 8  synthesis   729     0.0265
#> 9      adapt   554     0.0201

The moves are unevenly used: consensus and plan account for about a quarter of the moves each, adapt and synthesis for 2% to 3%. A model that always predicts consensus is correct a quarter of the time, so the informative question is which histories change that default.

Common and divergent pathways

The pathway tables give the contexts of the tree in one schema: the pathway (oldest move on the left), its depth, its count, the most likely next move and its probability, the Kullback-Leibler divergence in bits of its next-move distribution from that of its parent, and whether the most likely next move differs from the parent’s (changes_prediction). common_pathways() ranks the contexts by count.

common_pathways(tree, top = 8)
#>             pathway depth count likely_next next_probability divergence
#> 1           (start)     0 27533   consensus            0.247         NA
#> 2         consensus     1  6329        plan            0.396   0.334030
#> 3              plan     1  6157        plan            0.374   0.234143
#> 4           discuss     1  3951   consensus            0.321   0.555626
#> 5           emotion     1  2837    cohesion            0.325   0.555145
#> 6 consensus -> plan     2  2336        plan            0.375   0.000648
#> 7      plan -> plan     2  2108        plan            0.376   0.000432
#> 8        coregulate     1  1970     discuss            0.274   0.180891
#>   changes_prediction
#> 1                 NA
#> 2               TRUE
#> 3               TRUE
#> 4              FALSE
#> 5               TRUE
#> 6              FALSE
#> 7              FALSE
#> 8               TRUE

The most frequent histories are the single moves and the pairs formed by consensus and plan. Their divergences are small at depth 2: after consensus -> plan the next move is predicted almost exactly as after plan alone (0.0006 bits). divergent_pathways() ranks by divergence instead.

divergent_pathways(tree, top = 8)
#>                             pathway depth count likely_next next_probability divergence
#> 1 synthesis -> discuss -> consensus     3    10  coregulate            0.596      0.940
#> 2     consensus -> cohesion -> plan     3    12        plan            0.827      0.926
#> 3                         synthesis     1   652   consensus            0.463      0.892
#> 4    cohesion -> discuss -> emotion     3    10    cohesion            0.496      0.872
#> 5                             adapt     1   509   consensus            0.474      0.789
#> 6     monitor -> monitor -> discuss     3    12     discuss            0.249      0.783
#> 7 cohesion -> cohesion -> consensus     3    19        plan            0.366      0.756
#> 8  coregulate -> emotion -> monitor     3    13   consensus            0.382      0.752
#>   changes_prediction
#> 1               TRUE
#> 2              FALSE
#> 3              FALSE
#> 4               TRUE
#> 5              FALSE
#> 6               TRUE
#> 7              FALSE
#> 8               TRUE

Six of the eight most divergent contexts are three-move histories seen 10 to 19 times, close to the minimum of ten that the fit allows. After consensus -> cohesion -> plan, for example, plan follows with probability 0.83, against 0.36 after cohesion -> plan, but the estimate rests on 12 occurrences. A large divergence on a small count is the pattern that pruning and the bootstrap are designed to test: it may reflect a real routine or a handful of sequences.

Smoothing and pruning

Each node carries a smoothed distribution; the default floor smoother leaves a fully observed distribution unchanged and gives every unobserved next move a probability of 0.001. Pruning then removes the contexts whose history does not change the prediction of the parent by more than chance. compare_pruning() applies the four criteria to the same tree.

compare_pruning(tree)
#>   criterion n_nodes reduction_pct
#> 1        G2      23          93.9
#> 2        KL     368           2.4
#> 3       AIC      20          94.7
#> 4       BIC      10          97.3

The likelihood-ratio criterion G2 keeps 23 of the 377 contexts; AIC keeps 20 and BIC 10, while KL, at its default threshold of 0.005 nats, keeps almost all of them. Most of the grown depth is therefore not supported. The tree pruned with G2 at α=0.05\alpha = 0.05 is used below.

pruned <- prune_tree(tree, criterion = "G2", alpha = 0.05)
pruned
#> <transitiontrees>  23 nodes, depth <= 3, 9 states  [pruned]
#>   alphabet : adapt, cohesion, consensus, coregulate, discuss, emotion, monitor, plan, synthesis
#>   fit on   : 2000 sequences, 27533 observations
#>   smoothing: floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate)   min_count = 10
#>   pruned by: G2   alpha = 0.05
#> (start)   n=27533  -> consensus (0.25)
#> |-- adapt     n=509    -> consensus (0.47)
#> |-- cohesion  n=1695   -> consensus (0.50)
#> |   `-- cohesion  n=45     -> consensus (0.42)
#> |-- consensus  n=6329   -> plan (0.40)
#> |   |-- cohesion  n=795    -> plan (0.38)
#> |   |   `-- cohesion  n=19     -> plan (0.37)
#> |   `-- emotion   n=830    -> plan (0.39)
#> |       `-- emotion   n=58     -> plan (0.62)
#> |-- coregulate  n=1970   -> discuss (0.27)
#> |-- discuss   n=3951   -> consensus (0.32)
#> |   |-- adapt     n=29     -> adapt (0.24)
#> |   `-- coregulate  n=486    -> consensus (0.32)
#> |       `-- discuss   n=88     -> consensus (0.27)
#> |-- emotion   n=2837   -> cohesion (0.33)
#> |   |-- emotion   n=199    -> cohesion (0.35)
#> |   `-- plan      n=831    -> consensus (0.33)
#> |       `-- cohesion  n=33     -> cohesion (0.27)
#> |-- monitor   n=1433   -> discuss (0.38)
#> |-- plan      n=6157   -> plan (0.37)
#> |   `-- cohesion  n=221    -> plan (0.36)
#> |       `-- consensus  n=12     -> plan (0.83)
#> `-- synthesis  n=652    -> consensus (0.46)

The pruned tree keeps the root, the nine single moves and 13 longer histories. Smoothing and pruning gives the formulas of the five smoothers and four criteria.

Choosing the depth by cross-validation

In-sample criteria reward deeper trees. tune_tree() estimates the predictive quality of each configuration on data the tree has not seen: it divides the sequences into folds groups, fits on all but one, and computes the perplexity of the held-out group. The grid below crosses three depths with pruned and unpruned trees.

tuning <- tune_tree(group_regulation_long,
                    actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                    max_depth = 1:3, min_count = 10, prune = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                    folds = 5, seed = 1)
summary(tuning)
#> <transitiontrees_tune summary>  6 configurations, 0 with a failed fold
#> selected (minimum held-out perplexity):
#>  max_depth min_count                           smoothing prune perplexity n_nodes_avg
#>          1        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate) FALSE       5.46          10
as.data.frame(tuning, what = "grid")
#>   max_depth min_count                           smoothing prune logLik n_scored
#> 1         1        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate) FALSE -46738    27533
#> 2         1        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate)  TRUE -46738    27533
#> 3         2        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate)  TRUE -46763    27533
#> 4         3        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate)  TRUE -46884    27533
#> 5         2        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate) FALSE -47111    27533
#> 6         3        10 floor(ymin=0.001, rule=interpolate) FALSE -48782    27533
#>   perplexity n_nodes_avg folds_failed
#> 1       5.46        10.0            0
#> 2       5.46        10.0            0
#> 3       5.47        12.2            0
#> 4       5.49        23.4            0
#> 5       5.53        79.6            0
#> 6       5.88       344.4            0

The lowest held-out perplexity, 5.46, belongs to the first-order tree. The pruned trees of depth 2 and 3 are within 0.03 of it, whereas the unpruned depth-3 tree reaches 5.88: without pruning, the deeper contexts fit noise that does not recur in new sequences. For predicting the next move, one move of history is enough in these data; the longer contexts that survive pruning add little predictive accuracy, although they may still be of substantive interest. Model selection covers the tuning grid, the information criteria and the stability of the selection across fold assignments.

Assessing fit

model_fit() returns the log likelihood, the number of free parameters df (the number of contexts times the number of states minus one), the number of predicted moves, AIC, BIC and perplexity in one row.

rbind(unpruned = model_fit(tree), pruned = model_fit(pruned))
#>          logLik   df  nobs   AIC    BIC perplexity
#> unpruned -45465 3016 27533 96962 121763       5.21
#> pruned   -46570  184 27533 93509  95022       5.43

The unpruned tree has the higher in-sample likelihood and the lower in-sample perplexity (5.21 against 5.43), but it spends 3,016 parameters to obtain them; both AIC and BIC favor the pruned tree with 184 parameters. The in-sample perplexity of the pruned tree is close to its held-out value in the tuning grid (5.49), which indicates that it does not overfit.

Reliability of the pathways

A context retained by pruning has passed a test in this sample. bootstrap_pathways() asks whether it would pass again: it resamples whole sequences with replacement, refits the tree on each resample, and reports for each pathway whether its count is stable and whether its likelihood ratio statistic against its parent exceeds the critical value in most resamples.

boot <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200, seed = 1)
boot
#> <transitiontrees_bootstrap>  200 resamples
#>   stability  : count in [0.50, 1.50] x observed, p < 0.05
#>   informative: G^2 > qchisq(0.95, df=k-1) = 15.51, threshold 0.80
#>   pathways   : 23 total, 22 stable, 14 informative, 13 both
#> 
#> top pathways (stable + informative first):
#>                           pathway depth count p_stability stability_rate stable
#>                         consensus     1  6329       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                              plan     1  6157       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                           discuss     1  3951       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                           emotion     1  2837       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                        coregulate     1  1970       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                          cohesion     1  1695       0.005              1   TRUE
#>                           monitor     1  1433       0.005              1   TRUE

#>                             adapt     1   509       0.005              1   TRUE
#>  discuss -> coregulate -> discuss     3    88       0.005              1   TRUE
#>  informative_rate informative mean_G2 ci_G2_lo ci_G2_hi
#>              1.00        TRUE  2945.0   2759.0   3139.1
#>              1.00        TRUE  2000.9   1858.1   2146.1
#>              1.00        TRUE  3047.2   2922.9   3217.9
#>              1.00        TRUE  2191.6   2020.7   2363.4

#>              1.00        TRUE   576.0    497.2    678.0
#>              0.94        TRUE    25.3     14.1     39.5
#> # ... 13 more pathways (use summary(x) for full table)

Of the 23 pathways of the pruned tree, 22 are stable and 14 informative; 13 are both: the nine single moves and four longer histories. as.data.frame() returns the bootstrap estimates of every pathway with percentile intervals; the longer histories are:

subset(as.data.frame(boot, what = "summary"), depth > 1,
       select = c(pathway, count, stable, informative, informative_rate,
                  ci_G2_lo, ci_G2_hi))
#>                              pathway count stable informative informative_rate ci_G2_lo
#> 10  discuss -> coregulate -> discuss    88   TRUE        TRUE            0.940    14.11
#> 11   emotion -> emotion -> consensus    58   TRUE        TRUE            0.960    13.81
#> 12                  adapt -> discuss    29   TRUE        TRUE            0.875     9.90
#> 13              cohesion -> cohesion    45   TRUE        TRUE            0.835    10.43
#> 15                   plan -> emotion   831   TRUE       FALSE            0.130     2.76
#> 16              emotion -> consensus   830   TRUE       FALSE            0.615     6.56
#> 17             cohesion -> consensus   795   TRUE       FALSE            0.700     7.82
#> 18             coregulate -> discuss   486   TRUE       FALSE            0.390     6.13
#> 19                  cohesion -> plan   221   TRUE       FALSE            0.220     3.91
#> 20                emotion -> emotion   199   TRUE       FALSE            0.775     9.08
#> 21       cohesion -> plan -> emotion    33   TRUE       FALSE            0.765     7.70
#> 22     consensus -> cohesion -> plan    12   TRUE       FALSE            0.635     7.41
#> 23 cohesion -> cohesion -> consensus    19  FALSE        TRUE            0.870     9.76
#>    ci_G2_hi
#> 10     39.5
#> 11     45.3
#> 12     43.0
#> 13     47.9
#> 15     20.5
#> 16     31.8
#> 17     37.0
#> 18     29.1
#> 19     28.0
#> 20     45.4
#> 21     40.4
#> 22     30.4
#> 23     42.3

The four longer histories that are both stable and informative are discuss -> coregulate -> discuss, emotion -> emotion -> consensus, adapt -> discuss and cohesion -> cohesion; their likelihood ratio statistic exceeds the critical value of 15.5 in 84% to 96% of the resamples. These are the contexts on which a claim about longer memory can rest. The divergent consensus -> cohesion -> plan is retained by pruning and its count is stable, but its statistic exceeds the critical value in only 64% of the resamples, so its departure from cohesion -> plan is not reproducible.

Pathway reliability describes the two criteria and the distribution of the resampled statistics.

Predicting the next move

predict() applies the longest-suffix rule: the prediction for a history is the distribution of the longest context in the tree that ends the history. With tidy = TRUE it returns one row per history with the matched context, the most likely next move and the full distribution.

histories <- list(c("plan", "consensus"),
                  c("discuss", "coregulate", "discuss"),
                  "monitor")
predict(pruned, newdata = histories, tidy = TRUE)
#>   id                          history                          context predicted
#> 1  1                plan -> consensus                        consensus      plan
#> 2  2 discuss -> coregulate -> discuss discuss -> coregulate -> discuss consensus
#> 3  3                          monitor                          monitor   discuss
#>   probability   adapt cohesion consensus coregulate discuss emotion monitor  plan
#> 1       0.396 0.00474   0.0149     0.082     0.1877   0.188  0.0727  0.0466 0.396
#> 2       0.271 0.12487   0.0010     0.271     0.1361   0.204  0.1474  0.0010 0.001
#> 3       0.375 0.01117   0.0558     0.159     0.0579   0.375  0.0907  0.0181 0.216
#>   synthesis
#> 1   0.00758
#> 2   0.11361
#> 3   0.01605

The first history is predicted from consensus alone, because the pruned tree holds no longer context ending in it; the second matches the full three-move context retained by pruning. Prediction and scoring covers scoring of whole sequences, imputation and the generation of new sequences.

Comparing high and low achievers

Naming the external grouping column in group fits one tree per group over a shared alphabet. The comparison uses depth 2, so that most contexts are observed often enough in both groups.

groups <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                       actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                       group = "Achiever", max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
summary(groups)
#> <transitiontrees_group summary>  2 groups
#> 
#>  group n_seq n_obs n_nodes max_depth pruned logLik  df  nobs   AIC   BIC perplexity
#>   High  1000 13721      74         2  FALSE -22787 592 13721 46758 51214       5.26
#>    Low  1000 13812      77         2  FALSE -22984 616 13812 47199 51840       5.28

Each group contributes 1,000 sequences, with 13,721 and 13,812 moves; the two trees have 74 and 77 contexts. compare_groups() tests two kinds of difference by permuting the group labels of whole sequences: whether, after the same history, the groups choose different next moves (behavioral, a count-weighted Jensen-Shannon divergence), and whether they reach the same histories at the same rates (usage, a G-squared homogeneity statistic).

comparison <- compare_groups(groups, iter = 99, seed = 1)
summary(comparison)
#> Group comparison: High vs Low (80 contexts, 99 permutations)
#>   behavioral omnibus: JSD = 1772.142 bits, p = 0.010
#>   usage omnibus     : G2 = 1356.46, p = 0.010
#>   pathways with a behavioral difference (adjusted p < 0.05): 28
#>   pathways with a usage difference      (adjusted p < 0.05): 43
#>   pathways whose modal next state differs between groups: 26

Both omnibus statistics exceed every one of the 99 permuted values (p = 0.01, the smallest attainable with 99 permutations), so high and low achievers differ both in what they do after a given history and in which histories they reach. The contexts ranked by behavioral divergence, with Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values:

head(as.data.frame(comparison, what = "pathways"))
#>                   pathway depth count_total count_High count_Low modal_High modal_Low
#> 1        adapt -> monitor     2          16          4        12    discuss   discuss
#> 2    monitor -> synthesis     2          22         11        11  consensus     adapt
#> 3 synthesis -> coregulate     2          26          4        22    emotion consensus
#> 4        adapt -> discuss     2          29          4        25  consensus     adapt
#> 5       plan -> synthesis     2          11         10         1  consensus     adapt
#> 6    synthesis -> discuss     2          36          7        29  consensus synthesis
#>   flips jsd_bits jsd_p jsd_padj usage_g2 usage_p usage_padj
#> 1 FALSE    0.381  0.15    0.279 4.12e+00    0.05     0.0823
#> 2  TRUE    0.350  0.11    0.244 3.92e-04    0.95     0.9622
#> 3  TRUE    0.316  0.09    0.218 1.36e+01    0.01     0.0198
#> 4  TRUE    0.269  0.43    0.583 1.68e+01    0.01     0.0198
#> 5  TRUE    0.189  0.86    0.913 8.63e+00    0.02     0.0367
#> 6  TRUE    0.179  0.41    0.575 1.43e+01    0.01     0.0198

Comparing groups explains the two statistics, the stratified permutation for nested data and the plots of group differences.

Reporting

A report of this analysis states the data and session rule, the fitted and selected configurations, and the evidence for each claim, for example:

Regulation moves were modeled as a variable-order Markov chain with a prediction suffix tree (Ron, Singer, & Tishby, 1996). Moves were grouped into one sequence per student and session (gap > 900 s), giving 2,000 sequences and 27,533 moves over nine codes. A tree of depth 3 (contexts observed at least ten times; floor smoothing, ymin=0.001y_{\min} = 0.001) was pruned by likelihood-ratio tests at α=0.05\alpha = 0.05, which retained 23 of 377 contexts. Five-fold cross-validation favored one move of history (held-out perplexity 5.46; pruned depth 3: 5.49). In 200 bootstrap resamples, 13 pathways were stable and informative, four of them longer than one move. High and low achievers differed in next-move choices given the same history and in the histories they reached (permutation tests with 99 permutations, both p = 0.01).

References

Bühlmann, P., & Wyner, A. J. (1999). Variable length Markov chains. The Annals of Statistics, 27(2), 480–513. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1018031204

Ron, D., Singer, Y., & Tishby, N. (1996). The power of amnesia: Learning probabilistic automata with variable memory length. Machine Learning, 25(2–3), 117–149. https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1026490906255
